title: The gourd and the saved city
hookLine: Yunus is cast ashore, sick, and shaded by a gourd vine, and the people he walked away from turn back and are spared
tomorrow: Mecca, a valley of trade and idols

lines: A BARE SHORE, A SICK MAN.
cards: A bare shore. Allah cast him there while he was sick: the Qur'an tells it in a single line, and that's all it says. A man lying on the sand under a hard sun, weak, barely able to lift his head.

No shade, no food, no one. The man who walked out on his people has nothing left at all. And then, right over him, something begins to grow: a vine with wide green leaves, spreading over his body like an umbrella.
The Qur'an names the plant. It's a gourd.

teach.h: A TREE OF GOURD ABOVE HIM.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: “And We caused a tree of gourd to grow above him.” In Arabic, yaqtin.
Commentators explain it as a fast-growing gourd with broad leaves, the kind that gives quick shade and keeps flies away from a sick man's skin. A small mercy, sized exactly to what he needed.
Then the Qur'an turns to the part Yunus never saw coming: “And We sent him to a hundred thousand (folk) or more.” And they believed.
The people he walked out on, the ones he was sure would never listen, turned back to Allah. Surah Yunus, the tenth surah, the one named for him, singles them out.

teach.h: THE TOWN THAT TURNED IN TIME.
teach.b: It wishes aloud that the other towns warned of old had believed in time, as the people of Yunus did.
When they believed, the punishment was lifted from them, and they were given enjoyment of life for a while.

Commentators say the people went out together, men, women and children, and cried to Allah when they saw the warning signs, and they were spared. Yunus left because he was certain they wouldn't change. And they changed.
In the Qur'an's stories of warned towns, this is the one the text holds up as turning around in time.

And that closes week eleven: a messenger in the eastern place, a palm tree, a baby who spoke, Isa by Allah's leave, a man who left in anger, three darknesses, and a gourd vine over a city that believed.

how: Muslims read the end of Yunus's story in Surah As-Saffat and Surah Yunus, and it is often recalled as a reminder that no one should despair of a people turning back to Allah.

games.q: Yunus lies on the shore, sick, under a gourd vine. the people he walked out on, the ones he was sure would never change: what happened to them?
games.why: they believed, a hundred thousand or more, and were given enjoyment of life for a while (37:147–148; 10:98).

practice: Think of something you walked away from, or someone you gave up on: a friendship, a project, a skill, a relative.
Picture it now, without the old certainty that it would never change, and let the question sit: what if it has changed, or what if you have? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open the way.

wordCard.voice: Yaqtin, gourd: the vine that grew to shade sick Yunus, in the same story where the city he gave up on believed.

carryVoice: Your line: the city believed. Tomorrow, the stories of the prophets arrive in a valley called Mecca. Eleven weeks on the path.
